doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

title: Transcriptions of solos
summary: Written transcriptions do not look like what he played; academic over-explaining of notes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: It is and something you said just made me think of the number of times I’ve read about, usually a saxophone player — someone transcribes their uptempo solo, they give it to them and, “I can’t play that.”

Yup. Yup. I’ve seen transcriptions of something I’ve played and it doesn’t seem familiar to me. It doesn’t sound like something I would have played, or it doesn’t look — that’s the difference — it doesn’t look like something I would have played.
Explain a little more. Why doesn’t it look like it?

Well because when it’s written out it becomes, it’s a symbolic approach to something that was just a gesture. I mean like you and I are talking right now, but if we saw a transcription of what we’re saying, which we might well one day see, it would exist, it wouldn’t have the qualities or the character of what we’re experiencing here. And I’d probably look at it, you might look at it and go, “Oh jeez, that was stupid, why did I say that?” You know? It’s the same thing.

Have you ever had someone not only transcribe your solo but try to explain it? I’m thinking of some of these solos that — I sometimes think some of these Ph.D. candidates have to do some publishing and they’ll take a solo and there’ll be a phrase where they just have to find a way to justify a note.
It simply could have been an unintended note but damn it we’re going to figure out a way to call it something.
